subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Conditional Cooperators
description: A quick win: understand Conditional Cooperators.

hook.text: In lab experiments, 60% of people cooperate if they believe others will too. Only 10% are unconditional free riders.

buildup.text: Most people are conditional cooperators. They start cooperating and continue only if they see others doing the same.

discovery.text: Fischbacher used strategy method experiments. Subjects revealed cooperation rules before seeing others, confirming.

twist.text: One visible free rider can collapse a whole group. Conditional cooperators withdraw when they see others cheat.

climax.text: To sustain cooperation, make contributions visible and deal with free riders early.

punchline.text: Most people will cooperate if they trust others will too.

quiz.question: What are conditional cooperators?
options: People who never cooperate under any conditions
People who cooperate only if they believe others will too
People who always cooperate regardless of what others do

details.summary: Most people are conditional cooperators who will contribute to public goods and follow social norms as long as they believe others are doing the same. Cooperation collapses not because people are selfish but because they fear being the only one cooperating.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding conditional cooperation transforms policy design. Instead of assuming people need punishment to cooperate, effective policies simply need to credibly signal that most others are already cooperating to sustain public contributions.
takeaways: About 50 to 60 percent of people are conditional cooperators
Cooperation depends on beliefs about others' behavior, not just incentives
Showing that most people cooperate increases cooperation further

faq.question: What triggers the collapse of conditional cooperation?
faq.answer: When conditional cooperators observe or suspect that others are free-riding, they reduce their own contributions to avoid being exploited. This triggers a downward spiral where each person's reduced cooperation further reduces others' willingness.

faq.question: How can conditional cooperation be sustained in organizations?
faq.answer: Transparency about collective contributions, visible recognition of cooperators, and quick sanctioning of free-riders all signal that cooperation is the norm. When people trust that others are contributing fairly, they continue doing so.
